title: Your First Swap on an AMM
objectives: How a swap settles against a pool instead of a counterparty
What slippage tolerance protects you from, and what a loose setting costs
Why your own trade moves the price before you finish reading the quote

steps.title: Trading without a middleman
steps.body:
On a stock exchange your order passes through a broker, a clearing house, and opening hours. On Solana a <Term id="swap">swap</Term> is a transaction against a pool of tokens, and it settles in about a second, from any country, at any hour.

The pool is the counterparty, and a pool is just two stacks of tokens. An <Term id="amm">AMM</Term> prices it with a formula instead of an order book, which is why there's always a quoted price and never a waiting list for a buyer.

When you ask for a <Term id="quote">quote</Term>, you're being shown three things: the pool's current ratio between the tokens, the output that ratio predicts for your size, and the <Term id="price_impact">price impact</Term> your order will cause. That third one is the one people skip, and it's the one that matters most for a large trade.

A quote is an estimate, not a promise. It's computed from the pool's state at the moment you ask, and other traders can move that state before your transaction lands. That gap is exactly why slippage exists.

steps.title: Slippage is a floor, not a target
steps.body:
Because your transaction takes a moment to land, the pool can move underneath it. Slippage is the protection against being filled at a worse price than you agreed to.

Your <Term id="slippage">slippage tolerance</Term> - a number like 0.5% or 1% - sets a floor. It tells the contract: if the output would come in below this minimum, cancel the whole swap and return my tokens. Nothing partial, nothing "close enough".

Choosing the number is a real trade-off, and the usual instinct is backwards. Too tight and your transaction reverts constantly on volatile pairs - you pay fees and get nothing done. Too loose and you've published exactly how far a <Term id="sandwich_attack">sandwich attack</Term> can push the price while still filling you. A bot reads your tolerance as a budget.

For a liquid pair, 0.5% is a sensible default. The number is a safety floor, not something to maximise.

steps.title: What the pool does to your trade
steps.body:
Let's do it with numbers. Picture a pool holding 100,000 of token A and 100,000 of token B. Their product is 10,000,000,000, and the pool keeps that product constant after every trade. That's the only rule it enforces.

You swap in 1,000 A. The pool now holds 101,000 A. To hold the product steady it needs 10,000,000,000 ÷ 101,000 ≈ 99,009.9 B left over, so it pays you out 100,000 − 99,009.9 = 990.1 B.

Look at the price. Before the trade, one A bought one B. After it, 1,000 A bought 990.1 B - roughly 1% worse per B than the screen showed. Same pool, same formula, and your own order did that, before anyone else touched it.

That is price impact. It's why large orders in thin pools get punished: the swap doesn't fail, it simply fills worse as it eats through the reserves. Real pools also skim a fee per trade, usually around 0.25-0.3%, so the real output lands a little under the pure math above.

At the instruction level none of this is mysterious. You pass `amount_in` and a `min_out`. The program computes `amount_out` from the reserves, checks that `amount_out >= min_out`, and reverts if it isn't. The pool will never let you fill below the floor you set.

questions.prompt: What does a 1% slippage tolerance actually do?
options: Guarantees you a 1% profit on the trade
Fills only if you receive at least 99% of the quote, otherwise cancels
questions.explainRight: It sets your minimum output. Below that, the swap reverts instead of filling.
questions.explainWrong: It is a floor. If the price moves past it, the trade cancels rather than filling badly.

questions.prompt: Why does a token's price rise inside an AMM when someone buys it?
options: The developers adjust the price by hand
The buy removes that token from the pool, so each remaining one costs more of the other side
questions.explainRight: Buying drains the token from the reserves, and the formula makes each remaining unit cost more.
questions.explainWrong: The buy removes supply from the pool, so the math raises the cost of what's left.
